label: Educational mode. Plain-language lessons over the same engine as the planner. Every number shown comes from the model and is an estimate, not a measurement.

topics.title: RSSI (received signal strength)
topics.summary: RSSI is how strong a signal arrives, in dBm. Closer to zero is stronger: -50 dBm is excellent, -70 dBm is usable, -85 dBm is close to unusable.
topics.try_it: Move the probe over the plan and read the RSSI line. Then move an access point and watch it change.
topics.model_limit: The planner computes RSSI from a distance-and-wall model. A real device also depends on its antenna and orientation.

topics.title: SNR (signal to noise)
topics.summary: SNR is the signal level minus the background noise level, in dB. Higher SNR lets the radio use faster modulation. Without other interference, noise is mostly the receiver's own noise floor.
topics.try_it: Open the Dashboard tab and compare the RSSI histogram with the throughput estimate. Throughput follows SNR, not RSSI alone.
topics.model_limit: The noise floor is a typical value from the configuration, not a measurement of your room.

topics.title: SINR (signal to interference plus noise)
topics.summary: SINR also counts interference from other access points on the same or nearby channels and from non-WiFi sources such as microwaves. It is the number that decides the modulation rate when the air is busy.
topics.try_it: Choose the SINR map layer. Then run the interference lesson and watch the mean SINR rise.
topics.model_limit: Interference is added as average power scaled by an estimated duty cycle. Real bursts vary from moment to moment.

topics.title: Attenuation (what walls cost)
topics.summary: Every wall, door and floor removes some signal. The loss depends on the material and the band: concrete and metal cost far more than drywall or glass.
topics.try_it: Probe a point behind a wall and read the list of walls crossed. Change that wall's material and probe again.
topics.model_limit: Each material has one typical loss per band. Real walls vary with thickness, wiring and moisture.

topics.title: Propagation (how signal spreads)
topics.summary: In free space the signal falls with distance. Indoors it falls faster, because of clutter and walls. The planner uses a log-distance model plus wall losses, with optional reflection modes.
topics.try_it: Move an access point toward a weak room and compare the coverage percentage before and after.
topics.model_limit: Reflections are first order only. Diffraction around corners is not modelled.

topics.title: Frequencies (2.4, 5 and 6 GHz)
topics.summary: Higher frequencies carry more data but fade faster and pass through walls worse. 2.4 GHz reaches farthest and is the most crowded. 5 and 6 GHz have more channels and shorter range.
topics.try_it: Switch the Band control between 2.4 and 5 GHz and read the probe again.
topics.model_limit: Band differences come from configured path-loss and wall values, typical for planning.

topics.title: Channels
topics.summary: A channel is a slice of the band. Two access points on the same channel share airtime. On 2.4 GHz only channels 1, 6 and 11 do not overlap.
topics.try_it: Open the Spectrum tab to see which channels are crowded, then change an access point's channel.
topics.model_limit: Overlap between channels uses a spectral-mask estimate, not a measured filter shape.

topics.title: Interference
topics.summary: Interference is any energy on your channel that is not your signal: neighbours, other access points of your own, microwaves and Bluetooth. It lowers SINR, and with it speed and reliability.
topics.try_it: Add an interference source from the toolbar near an access point and watch the SINR layer.
topics.model_limit: Sources are planning assumptions with a typical power and duty cycle.

lessons.title: Distance and walls (propagation)
lessons.goal: Raise the signal in the bedroom by moving the router closer.
lessons.limit: Moving a router also changes the signal elsewhere. Check the coverage number, not just one point.

steps.instruction: Drag the router toward the middle of the flat, or press Show me. The bedroom probe point is at 6 m, 5 m.

lessons.title: Choosing a band (frequencies)
lessons.goal: See that 5 GHz is weaker than 2.4 GHz at the same spot.
lessons.limit: 5 GHz also offers more channels and less crowding, which this lesson does not show.

steps.instruction: Set the Band control to 5 GHz, then read the probe at the bedroom point (6 m, 5 m). It drops by about 12 dB.

lessons.title: What a wall costs (attenuation)
lessons.goal: Find the wall that blocks the bedroom and see what a lighter material would do.
lessons.limit: This is an experiment on the model. Do not take down real load-bearing walls.

steps.instruction: Probe the bedroom point (6 m, 5 m) and read the walls crossed. Change the concrete wall between the rooms to drywall.

lessons.title: Sharing the air (channels)
lessons.goal: Give the three office access points channels that do not overlap.
lessons.limit: Real offices also hear neighbours you cannot control.

steps.instruction: All three access points sit on channel 1 and hear each other. Set them to channels 1, 6 and 11, or press Show me.

lessons.title: Noise from a microwave (interference)
lessons.goal: Raise the mean SINR by removing the microwave.
lessons.limit: A real microwave only runs while in use. The model uses an average duty cycle.

steps.instruction: Select the microwave source and delete it, or press Show me. Mean SINR over the floor should reach 20 dB.

lessons.title: Closing a dead zone (SINR and coverage)
lessons.goal: Remove the dead zone between the racks.
lessons.limit: A new access point also needs a cable and power, which the model does not check.

steps.instruction: Add an access point in the middle of the racks (about 20 m, 12.5 m), or press Show me. The dead zone should drop to 2% or less.
